rv.q: Ryan Murphy's staging of 'The Boys in the Band' succeeds completely in bringing Mart Crowley's landmark 1968 play back to urgent, uncompromising life.
Happily, a lot about the play now seems dated — but not everything, and not in all circles of society, which makes this anniversary presentation doubly welcome.
These mean boys make the "Mean Girls" onstage a few blocks uptown in the Tina Fey hit seem like pussycats.
When it works best, it’s hilarious and vicious, like the subtext of Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf had split for New York City and decided to throw its own shindig.
At its most effective, Mantello's The Boys in the Band moves beyond the gay past and stares the present straight in the face.
They lock The Boys in the Band just outside the major works of its era, even if they can’t keep us away from the party.
Sometimes you have to see it all unveiled before you at once.

Bravely, the new production sticks pretty closely to the original, not even sanitizing the flippant racism directed at the one black character. (Some trimming has been done, and a few cosmetic changes have been made here and there: a reference to the operetta "The New Moon" has been changed to the less arcane "Funny Girl.
In a way, a production this shiny is always going to be more commemoration than eviscerating reinvestigation.
The revival of Mart Crowley's groundbreaking 1968 play about gay men in New York feels both dated and timeless, with a cast that brings genuine warmth to what could have been a museum piece.
But in mannerisms and voice, this guy is too tight, too cautious to be the extravagant, escapist playboy he is said to be.

And, as troubled as they may be, these boys offer splendid company on Broadway.
1968 was a momentous year for so many reasons. But one event that escapes most historical retrospectives was the premiere of what’s largely considered the first play about gay men in America.

When Alan first arrives at the party, the seismic shift in the gay men as they quickly put on their collective straight face is worth the price of admission, and should be seen by anyone who doesn’t know the devastating effects of the closet.

His script is still funny and cutting and heartbreaking, too; it’s also a fraught, glittering showcase for actors, which undoubtedly helped lure a top-line cast that includes Jim Parsons, Matt Bomer, Zachary Quinto, and Andrew Rannells.

Witnessing a rising class of out A-listers sink their teeth into the self-loathing, shame, and desire that have coursed through generations of gay identity is a truly transcendent experience — even if it doesn't quite tear up old scars.
Mantello and the cast have done a wonderful, respectful, and intelligent job bringing it back.
It still packs a wallop — even with slow patches and plot devices as old as the hills.
But it’s the creaky dramatics, not the changed mores, that make Boys in the Band feel like it’s playing such an odd tune.
The acting and direction are strong and precise, Crowley’s bitchy wisecracks are dropped like nasty bombs exactly on target.

cn.t: This starry 50th anniversary revival of Crowley's landmark 1968 play earns mostly positive reviews for its sharp wit and strong performances, though some critics question whether its depiction of gay self-loathing feels dated today.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.
